title: Self-Corrective RAG Engine
eyebrow: An answer should earn your trust.
description: A retrieval assistant that checks relevance, grounding, and usefulness before returning an answer.
problem: A retrieved document is not automatically a useful source. A fluent answer can still miss the question or go beyond the evidence.
solution: Route the question, retrieve context when needed, evaluate the evidence, and run a bounded correction path before returning a response or fallback.
features: Relevant, grounded, and useful answer checks
Bounded correction and conversational thread state
sourceStatus: Repository sources checked via GitHub, 20 Oct 2026

metrics.label: Local successful-answer latency
metrics.note: README-reported local observations on four questions; not a production latency guarantee.

metrics.label: Local fallback observation
metrics.note: README-reported single fallback observation; not a service-level objective.

architecture: A question and stable thread ID enter the non-streaming /chat API.
Conditional intent routing decides whether retrieval is needed.
Pinecone retrieves indexed context using Gemini embeddings.
LangGraph checks relevance, grounding, and usefulness; correction is bounded.
The API returns answer text. Pipeline exceptions can return HTTP 503.
challenges: Avoiding unconditional retrieval
Conditional routes use retrieval when the question needs project evidence.
Containing correction loops
Bounded correction prevents unending retries when evidence is insufficient.
Separating service and model health
GET / reports service status. Only a real chat request exercises downstream AI services.
limitations: Verification reduces risk; it does not establish zero hallucinations.
MemorySaver is process-local; server restarts can reset conversational memory.
Render may cold-start. API requests are rate-limited to 10 per minute per IP.
The experimental streaming route is not used by this portfolio.
questions: How does Navnit’s RAG engine check whether an answer is grounded?
What are the trade-offs of process-local conversation memory?

title: NeuroScan AI
eyebrow: From MRI slices to a spatial picture.
description: A 3D brain-tumor segmentation pipeline with interactive slice views and volumetric estimates.
problem: Brain MRI is a volume, not a single image. Full-volume processing is expensive, and 2D views can lose spatial relationships.
solution: Use a MONAI 3D U-Net with patch-based training and sliding-window inference, then explore the predicted region in three anatomical views.
features: FLAIR MRI input and 128³ patch processing
Axial, coronal, and sagittal slice exploration
Volumetric tumor estimation and NIfTI export
source: BRAIN_TUMOR_SEGMENTATION · README.md; owner validation attestation in implementation specification
sourceStatus: README checked via GitHub, 20 Oct 2026; validation result is owner-reported

demo.source: Recorded in the original frontend; availability not verified

metrics.label: Best validation Dice · owner-reported
metrics.note: 88.42%, reported by the owner/developer after more than two days of experimentation and 24+ hours of compute. Not independently substantiated by checked README/logs; not clinical validation.

architecture: Prepare spatial patches and transforms for the segmentation model.
MONAI/PyTorch predicts segmentation with spatial context.
Process the volume in overlapping 128³ windows; ONNX supports exported inference.
Inspect three slice planes, estimate volume, and export NIfTI masks.
challenges: Working within memory limits
Patch processing and sliding-window inference avoid loading a full-volume model pass at once.
Learning sparse tumor regions
Positive and negative crop sampling balances useful foreground and background examples.
Making output inspectable
Linked anatomical views and mask export make predictions easier to examine.
limitations: A research prototype, not a medical diagnostic tool or clinically validated system.
Validation performance does not establish generalization across scanners or populations.
No verified frame-rate claim or demo-availability guarantee.
questions: Why does NeuroScan use sliding-window inference?
What does the owner-reported Dice score tell us about NeuroScan?

title: Agentic Voice Booking Assistant
eyebrow: Let language understand. Let tools decide.
description: A voice-led booking workflow connecting selective retrieval, date validation, and correlated intake records.
problem: Voice conversations are flexible; appointment rules are precise. Asking a language model to calculate dates or enforce availability is fragile.
solution: Separate intent understanding from deterministic date and availability checks. Carry an intake_id from the call into the follow-up form to update the same record.
features: Voice-led booking across three clinic branches
Correlated intake forms, cancellation workflows, and model fallback
architecture: ElevenLabs captures the caller’s booking intent.
The agent coordinates tools and calls Pinecone for FAQ context when needed.
A deterministic workflow checks date and availability rules.
Supabase stores a partial record with an intake_id.
The form carries intake_id to complete the same record; operational flows handle cancellations.
challenges: Date arithmetic without prompt trust
Dedicated validation logic checks dates rather than relying on generated calculations.
Joining phone and form context
An intake_id correlates partial and completed booking data.
Handling operational changes
Separate workflows support emergency cancellation and fallback behavior.
limitations: Documented concurrency and slot-synchronization gaps remain.
Deterministic validation is a design choice, not a guarantee of perfect scheduling accuracy.
No supported public booking demo is documented.
questions: Why separate deterministic date tools from the voice booking agent?
How does intake_id connect voice calls to follow-up forms?

title: Fraud Detection
description: A transaction-classification project evaluated through the trade-off between missed fraud and false alarms.
problem: Fraud is rare. A high overall accuracy can hide a model that misses the cases that matter, while false alarms create a different cost.
solution: Build a classification workflow and inspect its held-out confusion matrix, making recall and false-positive rate visible alongside the model output.

metrics.note: Derived from README-reported FP=10 and TN=29,963: 10/29,973. No production fraud-detection guarantee.

architecture: Start with the project’s transaction dataset.
Use the saved classification pipeline to score transactions.
Inspect TN 29,963; FP 10; FN 4; TP 23 from the reported holdout.
Present the model result and evaluation context in Streamlit.
challenges: Evaluating rare events
Recall and false-positive rate expose behavior hidden by overall accuracy.
Communicating different error costs
The case study keeps missed fraud separate from unnecessary alarms.
limitations: Reported holdout results do not establish live financial performance.
Rare positive cases make evaluation sensitive to the split and decision threshold.
Candidate demo is recorded but has not been functionally verified.

title: Customer CLV & Churn

description: Paired churn classification and customer-value regression, with separate evaluation for each task.
problem: Retention combines two questions: which customers may leave, and what future value they represent. One score cannot answer both.
solution: Use distinct classification and regression models, then present customer risk and estimated value with task-specific evaluation.
features: Saved evaluation report for both tasks
Decoupled FastAPI/Streamlit architecture with batch prediction

title: Multimodal Lecture RAG
eyebrow: Find the moment behind the answer.
description: Lecture transcription and retrieval with timestamp citations that help a learner return to the source.
problem: A useful lecture explanation may be buried in a long recording. A summary alone does not help a learner locate the original context.
solution: Transcribe lecture content, retrieve transcript passages, and synthesize answers with timestamp references back to the lecture.
features: Gemini answer synthesis with source timestamps
sourceStatus: README and app.py checked via GitHub, 20 Oct 2026

demo.source: GitHub repository homepage; live app not verified

architecture: Start with lecture media for the transcription workflow.
Whisper produces transcript segments with timestamps.
Chunk and embed the transcript for retrieval.
Find context for the learner’s question; embedding consistency needs reconciliation.
Gemini synthesizes an answer with timestamp references.
challenges: Connecting answers to source moments
Timestamp references make the original explanation easier to revisit.
Reconciling embedding implementations
README describes Gemini embeddings; current app.py requests Hugging Face BAAI/bge-m3 query embeddings. Deployment consistency is unverified.
limitations: The README/code embedding mismatch must be reconciled before claiming a consistent deployed retrieval space.
Transcription and retrieval errors can affect answer quality.
No checked benchmark supports sub-second end-to-end retrieval or answering.
questions: How do timestamp citations help the lecture RAG project?
